newsitem.title: USA: Chile's Frei arrives for trade talks.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Frei arrives for trade talks.

text.p: Chilean President Eduardo Frei arrived on Tuesday for talks with President Bill Clinton and other U.S. officials on expediting Chile's inclusion in the NAFTA trade agreement.
Frei's plane landed at Andrews Air Force Base in nearby Maryland after a short flight from Chicago, where he spent the second day of his U.S. visit.

Clinton administration officials have said they would push hard for Congressional approval of fast track legislation to bring Chile into the North American Free Trade Agreement which links the United States, Canada and Mexico.
Frei meets Clinton on Wednesday and was expected to make his case for the fast track legislation when he addressed a joint session of Congress on Thursday.

"Complete trade liberalisation between Chile and the United States not only would strengthen our economic relations, but will also have a significant impact on the process of free trade in the Americas, which is an objective pursued by both countries," he told a business group in Chicago.
Frei also assured an audience at the University of Chicago that his country's military, while remaining independent, backed democratic rule.
"We chose to follow a road in 1988 to go back to democracy in a legal way. They (the armed forces) absolutely respect the democratic process ... and we respect the role of the armed forces," he said.
Frei was responding to a question about how Chile could be a true democracy if the military were independent and had its own budget.

The military seized control of Chile in a bloody 1973 coup under Gen. Augusto Pinochet in which President Salvador Allende died and his Socialist-Communist coalition was toppled. Thousands of Chileans were killed, jailed or exiled.

Pinochet lost a 1988 plebiscite and was forced to call elections the next year and hand over power in 1990. But he is still commander-in-chief of the army, which has raised concern that Chile's military are not accountable to civilian rule.

Frei said he wanted to correct a "falsehood going around" that Chile was building up its military. "Chile has one of the lowest investment in armament in the region, about 1.6 or 1.7 percent of the gross national product," he said.

"The only thing we do is maintain our sovereignty and replace old weaponry," he said. "We have arms suitable to protect our territory, our sovereignty. In Chile, we are moving ahead in our rightful and legal goals, and we have respect for the armed forces."
In his speech, Frei said Chile was "a nation governed by the rule of law, with independent powers and internal controls ... There is full respect for the law and personal rights are safeguarded."
